transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-15
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Dr. Emily Parker (CMO, Riverside), Jared Cole (Head of Eng), Maya Santos (AI/ML Lead)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align POC success criteria, workload sizing, benchmarks and timelines. Main focus: Quality evaluation plan - golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination/format checks, scoring approach.

Topics covered:
- POC goals and success criteria
- Workload & infra sizing expectations
- Benchmark setup and datasets
- Quality evaluation design (golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination detection, format validation)
- Timeline and next steps

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off - I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Priya Nair: Hi all, excited to dig into the quality plan. quick note, I'm going to talk through the benchmark harness and the eval metrics, and then we'll sync on what Riverside can provide for golden prompts.
[00:16] Dr. Emily Parker: Thanks Alex, thanks Priya. From our side Maya and Jared are on - main goal is to validate safety and clinical accuracy, also performance for integration into clinician workflows.
[00:26] Jared Cole: Hey. We're particularly sensitive to hallucinations and strict output formatting - a lot of our downstream systems rely on structured JSON, so format checks are key.
[00:34] Maya Santos: And we want an automated regression suite so we can detect model drift after updates.

-- Qualification / Success criteria --
[00:42] Alex Chen: To make this concrete: typical Redwood POCs we see have a set of success criteria mixing quality and performance. For Riverside I suggest we define primary and secondary criteria. Primary: clinical accuracy / hallucination rate and format correctness; Secondary: latency and cost.
[00:56] Dr. Emily Parker: Primary criteria should be: less than 3% clinically-significant hallucination on the golden set, and >= 95% schema-conformant outputs for structured replies. If those pass, we consider it a success.
[01:12] Priya Nair: That maps well. For latency, what's acceptable?
[01:15] Jared Cole: For the clinician UI, p95 under 300 ms is ideal, but we can accept up to 500 ms for complex generative tasks. For closed-loop alerts we want lower, but that's later.
[01:27] Alex Chen: Ok we'll capture that: p95 <= 300ms target for typical prompts, and a secondary objective p95 <= 500ms for heavy requests. We'll run hosted vs dedicated to show delta.

-- Workload sizing --
[01:38] Alex Chen: What throughput should we size for in the POC?
[01:41] Jared Cole: Baseline: 25 QPS peak for the first phase, average ~6 QPS. Token sizes vary - average request: 120 tokens input, 80 tokens output. Some workflows spike to 800 tokens output for summarizations.
[01:55] Priya Nair: Good to know. For benchmarking we'll include three buckets: small (<=128 tokens), medium (~500 tokens), large (>=800 tokens). We'll use a traffic mix file to simulate 70/25/5 percent distribution.

-- Benchmark environment & datasets --
[02:12] Priya Nair: We'll provide a benchmark harness (python) that can run on your infra or ours. It will measure throughput, p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and run quality checks (regression scoring). We'll need: golden prompts (we ask for 1,000 representative prompts), a broader test set (10k examples), and a set of adversarial/edge cases (~200) for hallucination checks.
[02:33] Maya Santos: We can produce 1k golden prompts within a week; we have a clinical team to annotate expected outputs. For the 10k set we can sample from historical interactions, redacting PHI.
[02:42] Alex Chen: Great. We'll provide the harness and a spreadsheet template for expected outputs. We'll also ask for gold labels where possible - if you can give expected fields for structured outputs that helps format validation.

-- Quality evaluation plan (deep dive) --
[02:55] Priya Nair: Here's the proposed eval plan:
[02:58] 1) Golden prompts: 1,000 high-priority prompts with expected outputs. For structured responses we validate against a JSON schema; for free-text we apply semantic similarity checks and clinical correctness labeling.
[03:12] 2) Regression tests: Run daily comparison of candidate model vs baseline on the 10k test set. Flag regressions if overall semantic-similarity drops by >2% or if hallucinations increase by >1 percentage point on clinical-critical items.
[03:28] 3) Hallucination detection: Multi-step approach - (a) automated heuristics + QA classifiers that flag unsupported facts, (b) entity-level grounding checks against a curated knowledge base, and (c) human review for sampled failures. Threshold: unacceptable if clinically-significant hallucination >3% on golden prompts.
[03:46] 4) Format checks: JSON schema validation for structured output, strict field presence checks, and normalization (dates, units). Failures counted as format errors. Pass criteria >=95% conformity.
[03:58] 5) Scoring approach: Mix of automatic metrics and human annotation. For free-text answers we'll compute embedding-based cosine similarity (use sentence-transformer baseline), BLEU/ROUGE as auxiliary, and a clinical correctness binary label from SME annotators for gold set. Overall score is weighted: SME correctness 60%, semantic similarity 25%, format 15%.
[04:21] Maya Santos: On scoring, can we see a worked example? How would a borderline answer be handled?
[04:25] Priya Nair: Yes - e.g., if SME label = pass (1) but semantic similarity is 0.78 (below our 0.85 target), the weighted score still might pass if SME weighs heavily. We will report per-item breakdown so you can decide to tune weights.

-- Golden prompts & expected outputs --
[04:40] Alex Chen: For golden prompts, we recommend categorizing by intent and clinical severity. Provide expected structured fields when relevant. Example: prompt: "Summarize this patient note and extract medication changes" -> expected JSON with fields [current_medications, stopped_medications, dose_changes].
[04:55] Dr. Emily Parker: We'll map those fields to our internal schema. We'll annotate 1k items prioritized by highest clinical impact.

-- Regression tests / baseline definitions --
[05:04] Priya Nair: Baseline model for the POC will be stable open model X (we'll provide model config). We'll capture a snapshot of outputs from baseline as the reference. Each new candidate model runs against same test set; we compute delta metrics.
[05:16] Jared Cole: Are we able to pin model versions and roll back automatically if regression crosses threshold?
[05:20] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood has rollout and automatic fallback policies - we can set a canary with traffic percentage and automatic fallback to baseline if regressions exceed configured thresholds. We'll show that in the console during pilot.

-- Hallucination & safety checks (examples) --
[05:32] Priya Nair: Detecting hallucinations in clinical domain is tricky. We will: 1) run an entity grounding pass - check medication names against drug DB and flag unknown meds; 2) run a factuality classifier trained on clinical QAs; 3) sample a fixed percentage (e.g., 5%) for human review, focusing on high-impact outputs. We will log confidence scores and produce an explainability trace per flagged item.
[05:52] Maya Santos: For meds and dosages we need very low false positives on hallucination detection, otherwise we'll drown in alerts.
[05:57] Priya Nair: Understood - we'll tune thresholds conservatively and present a confusion matrix.

-- Format validation (examples & tooling) --
[06:05] Priya Nair: For structured outputs we'll run JSON schema validation. We'll also run lightweight sanitization (dates normalized to ISO8601, units standardized). For failures we'll include specific error messages so engineering can map expected fields.
[06:16] Jared Cole: And will the harness return example failing items and diffs?
[06:19] Priya Nair: Yes, the harness outputs a per-example diff, the baseline vs candidate output, failed schema fields, and a simple UI-friendly CSV so your team can triage.

-- Scoring thresholds & acceptance gating --
[06:30] Alex Chen: Proposed acceptance gate for POC:
[06:33] - Clinical correctness (SME-reviewed golden set) >= 90%
[06:36] - Hallucination (clinically-significant) < 3% on golden set
[06:39] - Format conformity >= 95% on structured outputs
[06:42] - Latency p95 <= 300ms (hosted baseline) and documented improvement on dedicated if used
[06:47] - No critical security blockers (SOC2 controls in place)
[06:50] Dr. Emily Parker: Those look reasonable; we might push SME correctness to 92% for go/no-go, but fine to iterate.

-- Reporting & dashboards --
[06:59] Priya Nair: We'll surface results in the Redwood console: per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost breakdown, regression trend charts, and a quality dashboard that shows SME pass rates, hallucination counts, and format error rates. We'll also deliver a weekly benchmark report during the pilot.

-- Timeline --
[07:14] Alex Chen: Proposed timeline:
[07:16] - Day 0 (this week): share security docs and benchmark harness
[07:19] - +3 business days: Riverside shares golden prompts sample and test dataset plan
[07:22] - +7 business days: run initial baseline benchmarks on 1k gold set and report
[07:25] - +14 business days: run full 10k test set, report, and hold review call
[07:28] - Week of 2026-03-22: pilot kickoff with infra config and test runs scheduled
[07:31] Maya Santos: Sounds good; we need to sync with QA annotators availability - we'll confirm by Friday.

-- Risks / tradeoffs discussed --
[07:38] Jared Cole: Tradeoff we discussed: cutting latency with more aggressive quantization may increase hallucination risk. We need clear guardrails.
[07:45] Priya Nair: We'll include quantization profiles in the recommendations and measure quality delta in the regression tests. Also we'll test a multi-model routing policy so low-risk queries hit fast quantized models and high-risk clinical queries hit higher-precision variants.
[07:58] Alex Chen: Another operational risk is data residency - if you need VPC/private deployment we can run the POC in your VPC or provide a Private deployment. That affects setup time.
[08:07] Dr. Emily Parker: We will require VPC peering for the pilot; we have procurement rules around this.
[08:12] Alex Chen: Noted - that adds a few days for networking but is doable. We'll coordinate with your infra team.

-- Example eval item (walkthrough) --
[08:20] Priya Nair: Quick worked example: prompt: "Summarize patient visit and list med changes". Baseline output includes fields A,B,C. Candidate model output misses 'dose_changes'. Schema validation fails -> format error. SME labels candidate as clinically unacceptable for that item. That increments failure metrics and appears on the regression dashboard with the diff.
[08:40] Maya Santos: OK, we want those diffs surfaced as CSVs and direct links to raw text for reviewers.
[08:45] Priya Nair: We'll include those and sample annotation links.

-- Documentation & references --
[08:50] Alex Chen: We'll send: SOC2, architecture diagram, benchmark harness link, results template, and a sample scoring rubric.
[08:58] Dr. Emily Parker: Thanks. Also please include guidance on SME annotation interface and expected turnaround time per item.
[09:03] Priya Nair: We'll include a recommended workflow: SME reviews batched items of 50, estimated 2-3 minutes per item depending on complexity.

-- Closing / recap --
[09:13] Alex Chen: Quick recap: action items (send security docs, benchmark harness, Riverside to send golden prompts), acceptance gates (SME correctness ~90-92%, hallucination <3%, format >=95%, latency p95 <=300ms), proposed timeline (kickoff week of 3/22). We'll share the evaluation rubric and harness by Wednesday.
[09:30] Jared Cole: Thanks, that works. We'll circle back once we have the golden prompts ready.
[09:34] Maya Santos: I'll assign annotators and update you on Friday.
[09:38] Dr. Emily Parker: Appreciate the thorough plan.
[09:41] Alex Chen: Great - thanks everyone, we'll follow up over email with links and next steps.
